Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
You can never know who will harm you

vignette:
Marisol had been 59 when she finally agreed to come for help, but she traced the beginning of her distress back to the week she was taken and kept against her will several years earlier, an experience she still described in halting, concrete fragments rather than as a single story. She had been living as a divorced woman in the United States, working for years as a project manager, the kind of job that had once depended on her keeping meetings moving, coordinating people, and staying composed under pressure. During the captivity, what frightened her most was the combination of confinement and helplessness: being shut into a locked room, realizing there were no real options, no quick way out, no one she could persuade in the moment to let her leave. Even now, she could still picture the hard edges of the space and the way her body had gone rigid in it. The memory remained vivid enough that she did not need much to be pulled back into it. A door that closed with a lock, a cramped office with no easy exit, or even finding herself in a place where she had to wait without control over when she could leave would bring on a surge of dread. She said that the worst part was not just the room itself but the certainty, in those moments, that she had no options.

Afterward, Marisol found herself building habits around keeping the event at bay. At times she told herself the whole thing did not really happen or that it had not been as bad as it felt, as if reducing it in her mind might make it less present. More often, though, she went over and over the details, trying to make sense of every turn of the event, especially the points at which she believed she should have done something differently. She dwelled on what she had done wrong, replaying her decisions with a harshness that could go on for hours. She had come to believe that there was something fundamentally unsafe about people in ways she could not predict, and she would say, with a tired certainty, that you can never know who will harm you. That belief sat beside a different one she spoke about with sadness: she used to be a happy person, she said, but now she was always miserable, and at times she felt dead inside, as if part of her had gone numb and stayed that way.

Her symptoms showed themselves most clearly in the ordinary settings of her current life. As a project manager, she still had to attend meetings, review plans, and move through office buildings, but she became intensely uneasy if she was in a locked or confined room. She would notice exits immediately, choosing chairs closest to the door, and if a conference room felt too enclosed she struggled to take in what others were saying because she was monitoring the space instead. In her home, where one might expect comfort, she did not fully relax. She remained on guard even inside her own house, listening for sounds and reacting as if something were wrong when nothing actually was. A sudden knock, a noise in the hallway, or even an unexpected silence could make her startle and tense, as though danger had arrived without warning. She recognized that these were false alarms, yet that knowledge did not stop her body from responding as if she were again in the place where she had been trapped.

Marisol also noticed how her neck pain could pull the past into the present. When the discomfort flared, she would immediately think of being held captive, and the pain itself seemed to carry the memory of how tense and powerless she had felt then. That sensation made it harder for her to settle, especially at home after work, when she wanted to rest but could not fully let herself. Over time, the strain of these experiences changed her relationships and her routines. She became more selective about where she went and how long she stayed, often arranging her life around the possibility of being trapped or caught off guard. Her divorce already meant she lived alone, and the combination of isolation and vigilance made the evenings feel especially long.

By the time she sought treatment, Marisol was exhausted by the constant sense that she had to be prepared for harm. She came not because the memories had become distant, but because they remained too immediate: the locked room, the lack of options, the body tension in her neck, the scanning of her home, the inability to settle even in places she knew were safe. What brought her in was the fear that she could not keep living this way, and what she hoped for, quietly and with some uncertainty, was the chance to feel safe enough to stop bracing for the next danger.
